answer.exemplar: A gamma distribution describes the total time until a fixed number of independent events have occurred, each arriving at a constant rate, so it is the sum of a whole number of independent exponential waiting times rather than a single one. A model answer should say that a shape of 1 collapses to the exponential case, a shape of 3 means the time until the third event of a constant-rate process, and that because the stages are independent their means and variances add, giving a mean of shape over rate and a variance of shape over rate squared. It should also note the consequence that the shape is an integer count of stages, so a non-integer shape needs the extension to incomplete gamma functions, and that the memoryless property belongs to a single stage and not to the total.

questions.explanation: The stage reading is what makes the distribution concrete instead of algebraic, and it also produces the mean and variance by addition without any integration. Saying that the shape counts the number of events whose arrival is being awaited is the whole content of the model, and it separates a gamma from the exponential, which is the single-stage case. A model answer that only writes the formulas has not explained the process, which is what the format is asking for.
questions.hint: Describe the total as a sum of independent exponential stages and let the shape count the stages.

answer.exemplar: The sample mean is a weighted sum of many independent terms, and the shape of a sum is governed by its number of terms rather than by the shape of any one of them, so the summands get diluted. A model answer should say that independence prevents the extremes from lining up, and that the mean of n observations has a mean equal to the population mean and a standard error equal to the population standard deviation over the square root of n, so normalising by that quantity tends to the standard normal as n grows. It should add that only finite mean and finite variance are required of the population, that a heavy tail can still slow the convergence, and that the theorem says nothing about the population's own distribution, which may be badly skewed at every finite n.

questions.explanation: The dilution argument is the heart of it, and a model answer has to make it rather than assert that averaging makes things normal. The standard error formula is what supplies the shrinkage of the spread, and dividing by it is what turns the sum into a standardised quantity whose limit can be stated. The commonest weak answer stops at the central limit theorem being about sums and means, which is true but does not explain why the shape emerges or why the population need not be normal at all.
questions.hint: Focus on the number of independent terms, the standard error, and what happens to the population shape.
